headline: Big tech companies keep borrowing for AI even as bond yields rise, reversing the usual pattern in which costlier borrowing slows bond sales, Bloomberg reports.
score_reason: Pool score 6 kept: a data-backed Bloomberg analysis read in full; its claims are market trends resting on strategists' views.
importance_line: What changed is that AI borrowing keeps rising even as rates climb, leaving a steady flow of new debt for bond investors to absorb, which matters first to savers and pension holders who own corporate bonds, then to companies outside AI that are delaying bond sales over the higher cost, then to the big tech borrowers, and the doubt is that yields are also rising because of government borrowing and inflation fears, and the view that AI issuance will not slow rests on strategists' expectations.
summary: Bloomberg reports that US companies have sold $1.69 trillion of bonds so far this year, some 30% more than a year earlier, even as average yields (the interest rate investors demand) climbed about 1.2 percentage points to 5.97%, because big tech firms known as hyperscalers will pay more to borrow for AI data centers and chips; for a decade through 2025, bond sales tended to fall when yields rose. Other issuers are holding back, with US companies selling only $11.4 billion of notes this week against the $25 billion to $30 billion dealers expected, and reports of possible further financings by SpaceX and Broadcom have added to investor worries about the supply of new debt.
notes: Bloomberg page blocked (HTTP 403); full Bloomberg Credit Weekly text (by Tasos Vossos) read on Business Standard, which carries it, so Bloomberg is the source and the link is Bloomberg's original. The SpaceX and Broadcom financings were carried in our 7 and 8 Oct 2026 editions; this piece adds the supply figures and the break in the usual pattern.
